I'll write the explainer to about 900 words and check the count before sending it.A Raft cluster accepts new commands only while its servers agree on one leader. The leader appends each command to its log and replicates that log. Leader election picks this server and picks the next one after the current leader goes silent. A term has at most one leader, and later Raft rules rely on that.

Each server is a follower, a candidate, or a leader, and it starts as a follower. A follower does not start an election while a current leader's AppendEntries arrives or while it grants a vote. A candidate is collecting votes. A leader holds a majority and sends heartbeats so other servers stay followers.

## Terms

Raft divides time into terms, integers that only increase. Each term starts with an election. If a candidate wins a majority, it leads for the rest of that term. If no majority forms, the term has no leader, and the next term starts a new election. A partitioned server can skip terms, from 4 to 7, on the next message it accepts.

RequestVote and AppendEntries carry the sender's term. A server stores any higher term it sees, and if it is a candidate or a leader it becomes a follower. A server rejects a lower term and returns its own term, so the sender becomes a follower too.

## Heartbeats

A leader sends heartbeats to every other server for the whole time it leads. A heartbeat is an AppendEntries call with no log entries. The same call carries entries when the leader has commands to replicate. The gap between heartbeats is much smaller than the election timeout.

The 2014 Raft paper [RAFT] by Ongaro and Ousterhout requires broadcast time much less than the election timeout, and the election timeout much less than the mean time between failures of one server. Broadcast time is the time to send those calls in parallel and receive the replies. For example, the paper uses a random draw from 150 to 300 milliseconds.

A follower that receives a heartbeat for its current term restarts its election timer. If the heartbeat carries a higher term, the follower stores that term and follows the sender. A candidate ends its election if a leader's heartbeat has an equal or higher term. A heartbeat from an older term is rejected.

## Election timeouts

Each follower runs an election timer that starts when the server becomes a follower. The timer restarts if AppendEntries arrives from the current leader, and it restarts if the follower grants a vote. If the timer expires, the follower has seen neither, so it starts an election.

Each timer is a fresh random draw, so servers rarely expire together, and the shortest draw must exceed broadcast time. On expiry the follower adds one to its term, becomes a candidate, and votes for itself. It stores the term and the vote on stable storage, then sends RequestVote in parallel to every other server. The message carries the new term, the candidate id, and the index and term of its last log entry. It then starts another random timer. If that timer expires and no one has a majority, the candidate repeats this in the next term.

A server grants the vote only if every check passes. The candidate's term is at least the server's term. The server has not already voted for someone else in this term. The candidate's log is at least as up to date as the server's log. The log with the higher term on its last entry is more up to date. If the last terms match, an equal or longer log passes. A server missing committed entries therefore cannot win and overwrite them. The server stores the term and the vote on stable storage before it replies, and a restart still shows that vote as spent.

The candidate counts its own vote toward a majority of the configured cluster. Five servers need three votes, so a partition of two cannot elect a leader and the other three can. The winner becomes leader and sends heartbeats immediately. AppendEntries from an existing leader at an equal or higher term also ends the attempt, and the candidate becomes a follower. If the timer expires with no majority, the result is a split vote.

## Split votes

A split vote happens when more than one follower times out at nearly the same moment. Consider servers S1 to S5 after the old leader has gone silent. S1, S2, and S3 become candidates in the same new term, and each votes for itself. A server can vote once in a term, and only for the first valid candidate it sees. Suppose S4 votes for S1, S5 votes for S2, and S3 gets no extra vote. The totals are 2, 2, and 1. A majority of five is 3, so this term elects no leader.

No new command can commit, because that requires a leader. Two leaders cannot both exist, because two majorities would need six votes from five servers. The first candidate to expire moves alone into the next term. Suppose S2 expires first and sends RequestVote while S1 and S3 still wait. They see a higher term, become followers, and their previous self-votes do not carry into the new term. S4 and S5 have not voted in the new term either. S2 can take three votes and send heartbeats before the other timers fire. Equal timeouts can split again. The random interval usually leaves one candidate in the next round.

[RAFT]: https://raft.github.io/raft.pdf "Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version), 2014."
